compositions.title: The ship and the fish
compositions.text: On ðǣm strande sindon ðrīe męnn and ān scip. Sum mann cwið: “Hwā is se mann, ðe ðæt scip hæfð?” His gefēra cwið: “Se mann is mīn gefēra. Hē hæfð ðā fiscas, ðe wē sēoð.” “Hwǣm sęlst ðū ðone fisc?” “Ic sęlle hine ðǣm męnn, se ðe mē healp.” “Hwilc scip hæfð hē?” “Hē hæfð ðæt lȳtle scip, ðæt ðe ðū gesāwe.”
compositions.scope_note: New controlled dialogue, not attributed to a historical source. Three men are present; one asks his companion about the third man. Questions and subject/object relatives use only assigned new pronouns and earlier lexical systems. The genitive his refers back to the first speaker. The dative antecedent menn and nominative se in the relative deliberately have different cases.

teaching_examples.target: Direct yes/no question; finite verb before noun subject.

teaching_examples.text: Hwā hæfð ðæt scip? Hwone siehð se mann?
teaching_examples.target: Subject who versus accusative whom; explicit case contrast.

teaching_examples.text: Hwǣm sęlst ðū ðone fisc? Hwæs scip siehst ðū?
teaching_examples.target: Dative recipient and genitive possessor questions; no productive personal genitive promotion.

teaching_examples.text: Hwæt hæfð se mann? Hū swimð hē? Hwȳ swimð hē?
teaching_examples.target: Neuter object what, lexical how and lexical why; not general instrumental syntax.

teaching_examples.text: Hwilc mann hæfð ðæt scip? Hwæðer mann hæfð ðæt scip? Hūlic is ðæt scip?
teaching_examples.target: Which, which of two and what sort; the second sentence assumes two candidate men supplied in context.

teaching_examples.text: Sum mann hæfð scip. Sume męnn habbað scipu.
teaching_examples.target: Ordinary attributive singular/plural sum; no partitive construction.

teaching_examples.text: Hæfst ðū ǣnigne fisc? Gehwilc mann hæfð scip.
teaching_examples.target: Any in a direct question; each in an affirmative singular clause.

teaching_examples.text: Se ōðer mann hæfð ōðer scip. Se ilca mann hæfð ðæt scip.
teaching_examples.target: Other/another and same; full prior other morphology reused with new sense.
Strong self emphasizing the masculine nominative subject; personal-pronoun reflexivity remains distinct.

teaching_examples.text: Swilc mann is gōd. Swilce męnn sindon gōde.
teaching_examples.target: Inflected such, distinct from invariant swilce likewise; context identifies the kind of man.

teaching_examples.text: Se mann, ðe ðæt scip hæfð, is mīn gefēra.
teaching_examples.target: Invariant subject relative with a masculine singular antecedent.

teaching_examples.text: Ic geseah ðæt scip, ðe se mann hæfð.
teaching_examples.target: Invariant object relative; the internal noun subject stays nominative.

teaching_examples.text: Ic sęlle ðone fisc ðǣm męnn, se ðe mē healp.
teaching_examples.target: Dative antecedent but nominative relative se, governed within its own clause.

teaching_examples.text: Ic geseah ðone mann, ðǣm ðe ic healp.
teaching_examples.target: Accusative antecedent but dative relative with helpan.

teaching_examples.text: Ðū, ðe mē hulpe, sęle mē ðone fisc.
teaching_examples.target: Second-person relative agreement and singular command; no third-person substitution merely because English uses who.

teaching_examples.text: Se mann, ðæs scip ic geseah, is gōd.
teaching_examples.target: Genitive possessive relative: nominative antecedent mann, genitive relative ðæs, accusative possessed noun scip. Ordinary internal-clause case, without attraction.
